body_markdown:
Worry has a strange way of taking over our days. A small concern can become a long chain of imagined problems, and before we realise it, we have spent hours replaying conversations, predicting what might go wrong or trying to find solutions to situations that may never happen.


For people who experience persistent anxiety, switching off those thoughts can feel almost impossible. The instinct is often to keep thinking until a problem has been solved. Unfortunately, worrying does not always work that way. Sometimes, the more attention we give an anxious thought, the bigger and more convincing it becomes.


One simple idea offers a different approach: give worry a time limit.


The concept is straightforward. Choose a point in the evening when you deliberately stop engaging with your worries. Instead of continuing to analyse every concern late into the night, you tell yourself that worrying can wait until tomorrow.


It may sound almost too simple. Yet creating a boundary around anxious thinking can be a surprisingly useful psychological exercise.


## Why do we keep worrying?


Worry can create the illusion that we are doing something productive. When something is uncertain, our minds naturally want answers. We may believe that if we think about a problem long enough, we will eventually find the perfect solution.


But there is an important difference between problem solving and repetitive worrying.


Problem solving usually involves identifying an issue, considering realistic options and deciding what action to take. Worry often goes in circles. We imagine different negative outcomes, question our decisions and then revisit the same possibilities repeatedly.


This can leave the brain in a constant state of alertness.


The result may be difficulty relaxing, problems concentrating, irritability or trouble sleeping. Instead of preparing us for life, excessive worry can prevent us from properly experiencing it.


## The idea of a daily worry deadline


A useful experiment is to establish a personal "worry deadline".


For example, you might decide that after 6.30pm, you will no longer deliberately analyse stressful issues unless something genuinely requires immediate attention.


The goal is not to pretend that problems do not exist. Nor is it to force unpleasant thoughts out of your head.


Instead, the idea is to postpone them.


If a worrying thought appears in the evening, you can acknowledge it and remind yourself that you are allowed to return to it tomorrow. If necessary, write down the concern so that you do not feel responsible for remembering it.


This creates psychological distance between you and the thought.


Rather than saying, "I must solve this right now," you can say, "This is something I can think about tomorrow."


That small change in perspective can be powerful.


## At first, it may not work perfectly


Anyone trying this technique should expect some resistance.


An anxious mind is unlikely to accept a new rule immediately. You might decide that worrying stops at 6.30pm, only to find yourself analysing something at 7.15pm.


That does not mean the experiment has failed.


The important thing is to practise the boundary rather than demand perfection.


Perhaps you manage half an hour without getting caught up in anxious thinking. The next evening, you might manage an hour. Gradually, the period of mental quiet can become longer.


The aim is not to eliminate every anxious thought. Human beings naturally worry from time to time. The aim is to stop worry from occupying every available moment.


## What can you do during your "no-worry" hours?


The hours after your worry deadline should not simply become a battle against your thoughts. Instead, they can be filled with activities that signal to your brain that the day is winding down.


Reading, cooking, listening to music, spending time with family or friends, taking a gentle walk or watching something enjoyable can help create a transition between daytime responsibilities and rest.


A consistent evening routine may also make the boundary easier to maintain.


For example, you could spend 15 minutes earlier in the day writing down anything that needs attention tomorrow. Once it is on paper, there is less pressure to keep rehearsing it mentally.


You can then move towards activities that are deliberately unrelated to problem solving.


## The connection with sleep


One reason an evening worry boundary may be helpful is that worrying in bed can make it harder to switch into a restful state.


When your brain associates bedtime with reviewing problems, planning for possible disasters or mentally replaying the day, settling down can become difficult.


Creating an earlier opportunity to acknowledge concerns may help prevent them from following you into bed.


This does not guarantee better sleep, and people experiencing persistent insomnia or severe anxiety may need professional support. However, establishing a calmer transition into the evening can be one practical habit worth experimenting with.


## It is not about ignoring real problems


There is an important distinction between postponing worry and avoiding responsibility.


If you need to pay a bill, have an important conversation, arrange an appointment or deal with a genuine emergency, those things still need attention.


The purpose of a worry deadline is to prevent unnecessary mental repetition, not to encourage people to neglect important tasks.


A useful question is:


**"Is there something I can realistically do about this tonight?"**


If the answer is yes, take the necessary action.


If the answer is no, ask whether continuing to think about it tonight is actually helping.


Sometimes the most productive thing you can do is wait until morning.


## Giving your brain permission to pause


Perhaps the most useful part of this approach is the permission it creates.


Many people feel guilty when they stop thinking about their problems. They may believe that relaxing means they are being irresponsible or that constant concern proves they care.


But caring about something does not require thinking about it every minute.


Rest is not the opposite of responsibility. It can be part of being able to deal with problems effectively.


By creating a daily boundary around worry, you are effectively telling yourself that some problems can wait. Tomorrow will still be there. The issue can be reconsidered with a fresher mind.


Over time, that separation may help reduce the feeling that anxiety is in charge.


## A small experiment worth trying


If worry regularly follows you into the evening, consider choosing your own cut-off time for one week.


Before the deadline, spend a few minutes identifying concerns and writing down any practical actions you need to take the following day.


Once the deadline arrives, deliberately shift your attention elsewhere.


Do not judge yourself if anxious thoughts return. Notice them, acknowledge them and gently remind yourself that they have already been scheduled for tomorrow.


The objective is not to achieve a completely empty mind. It is to practise choosing where your attention goes.


That distinction matters.


We cannot always control which thoughts appear. We can, however, become better at deciding which thoughts deserve our attention right now.


Sometimes, the first step towards a calmer evening is simply giving yourself permission to stop worrying until tomorrow.


### Disclaimer


This article is intended for general information and educational purposes only. It is not medical or psychological advice and should not be treated as a substitute for professional assessment or treatment. If anxiety, persistent worry or sleep difficulties are significantly affecting your daily life, consider speaking with a qualified healthcare or mental health professional. Individual experiences with anxiety and coping techniques can vary.
